reasoning: What the evidence shows: A QA tutor asks which response wins when one follows the format and the other is more accurate. A QA tutor asks which response is better for a task requesting a JSON object when one response explains the content beautifully in prose. A tutor asks whether accuracy can outweigh ignoring the user's requested output structure. The current FAQ requires scoring format violations separately from factual accuracy and identifying whether the structure was mandatory. It establishes no universal accuracy-versus-format tie-break rule; when the actual pair and applicable guidance do not settle preference, the prompt and both responses are required for team lead confirmation. In the tutor's thread, the team lead asks for the exact formatting instruction so QA can verify whether it was mandatory before weighing the responses. An earlier batch's calibration follow-up recorded improved agreement in its reviewed sample, but one pair remained disputed because the packet did not establish whether the format constraint was mandatory. The record explicitly does not establish a universal accuracy-versus-format preference rule. The repeated questions leave a comparison process worth clarifying across the threads, while the supplied messages do not contain the complete prompts and response pairs needed to decide the individual preferences. The current content-quality rubric treats missing explicit required format or structure as a major instruction-adherence defect, while grading factual defects separately; these task-quality grades do not determine operational incident severity.
